1.x: This marks the transition of Jesus’ trial from the religious domain of the Jewish Sanhedrin to the civil authority of the Roman Empire. “When the morning was come…”: Under traditional Jewish jurisprudence (codified in the Mishna, Sanhedrin 4:1), capital trials had to be conducted exclusively in daylight hours. A death sentence pronounced at night was strictly illegal and invalid. Therefore, as dawn broke (~6:00 AM), the council reconvened in an official morning session to rubber-stamp and formalize the illegal verdict they had already reached in secret hours earlier (Mt 26:65-66). “..all the chief priests and elders of the people..”: The Sanhedrin, comprising the priestly aristocracy (Sadducees) and the lay elders/scribes (Pharisees), stood united in their hostility. Despite their deep theological disagreements with one another, they found common ground in their hatred of Jesus Christ. “..took counsel against Jesus to put him to death”: The morning strategy session was not aimed at re-evaluation his guilt or innocence; it was a tactical meeting (“took counsel”) to determine how to present Jesus to the Roman authorities in a way that would guarantee his execution.

2.x: “And when they had bound him…”: Although Jesus had already been upon his initial arrest in Gethsemane (Jn 18:12), they bound his hands afresh, treating him publicly as a dangerous criminal and condemned traitor to humiliate him before the watching crowds. “..they led him away..”: They marched him from the High Priest’s residence across Jerusalem to the Praetorium (either the Fortress Antonia near the Temple Mount or Herod’s Royal Palace), where the Roman governor resided when visiting Jerusalem for the Passover feast. “..and delivered him to Pontius Pilate the governor”: Pontius Pilate is one of the better-attested Roman officials connected with the NT. The Pilate Stone has an inscription that says: “Pontius Pilate, Prefect of Judea” confirming that Pilate really was the Roman authority governing Judea at the time. Even beyond this inscription, his identity is corroborated by first century non-Christian historians like Josephus, Philo of Alexandria, Tacitus, and of course, the gospels. Since Judea was under Roman occupation, Rome had revoked the Sanhedrin’s authority to carry out capital punishment (jus gladii, the right of the sword; Jn 18:31). While Jewish law prescribed stoning for blasphemy, the Sanhedrin could not execute Jesus themselves, hence they depended on Pilate’s verdict as the sole authority in the region to sentence a man to Roman crucifixion. By handing Jesus over to Pilate, the religious leadership fulfilled Jesus’ own prophecy in Mt 20:18–19: "The Son of man shall be betrayed unto the chief priests... And shall deliver him to the Gentiles to mock, and to scourge, and to crucify him." Both Jewish religious leadership and Gentile civil power united to condemn the innocent Son of God (Acts 4:27). Before their own council, they condemned Him for blasphemy because He claimed to be the Son of God (Mt 26:63–65). But knowing Pilate would not care about Jewish religious disputes (John 18:31), they shifted their charge before Rome to sedition and political treason—claiming Jesus made Himself a king in opposition to Caesar (Luke 23:2).

3.x: “Then Judas…when he saw that he was condemned..”: Judas may have naively assumed Jesus would miraculously deliver himself from the Sanhedrin, as he had done before (Lk 4:30). Seeing Jesus bound and officially handed over to Rome for execution shattered Judas’ illusions. “...repented himself…”: The Greek verb used here is “metamelomai,” which means to feel deep regret, remorse, or emotional pain after the fact. It is distinct from true gospel repentance (“metanoeo,” a genuine change of mind and heart leading to salvation). Judas experienced worldly sorrow, which centers on self-reproach, guilt, and fear of consequences, rather than godly sorrow, which leads to spiritual life (“For godly sorrow worketh repentance to salvation not to be repented of: but the sorrow of the world worketh death,” 2 Cor 7:10 KJV). “...brought again the thirty pieces of silver…”: Overcome with guilt, the money that had seduced him now felt like a lead weight on his soul. He tried to undo his crime by returning the bribe.

4.x: “I have sinned in that I have betrayed the innocent blood”: Judas utters a profound legal testimony to the absolute sinlessness of Jesus Christ. Even his betrayer, who knew him intimately in private life, could find no flaw or moral charge against him. “What is that to us? See thou to that”: The response of the religious leadership exposes the utter coldness and cruelty of self-righteous religion. They used Judas to accomplish their wicked plot, and once he was no longer needed, they cast him aside in his despair.

5.x: “And he cast down the pieces of silver in the temple…”: Judas threw the money into the Sanctuary (naos: the holy place reserved for priests). “..and departed, and went and hanged himself”: Overwhelmed by shame and lacking faith to seek Christ’s forgiveness, Judas committed suicide.

Atheists and Muslims often attack the Bible by exposing a supposed contradiction between Matthew’s account and Luke’s record in the Book of Acts regarding how Judas died and who bought the field: (1) Manner of Death: “Went and hanged himself” (Mt 27:5) or “Falling headlong, he burst asunder in the midst, and all his bowels gushed out” (Acts 1:18). (2) Purchase of Field: The chief priests bought the Potter’s Field with the silver (Mt 27:6-7) or Judas “purchased a field with the reward of iniquity” (Acts 1:18). These two verses can be easily harmonized: Matthew records the cause of death, while Acts describes the gruesome physical aftermath. Traditional accounts locate the death of Judas in the Hinnom Valley (Gehenna) south of Jerusalem. The terrain features steep, jagged rocky cliffs lined with olive trees hanging over sharp drop-offs. So the sequence of events would be as follows: First: Judas hanged himself (Mt 27:5); Second: Because of Jewish ceremonial laws during Passover, no one immediately took the body down, or perhaps the rope/branch broke under his body weight after decomposition set in. Third: His body fell from the high tree or cliff down onto the jagged rocks below, causing his swollen torso to rupture upon impact (Acts 1:18). Now, regarding who purchases the field: Matthew’s perspective gives the legal, direct account. He notes that Judas threw the silver into the Temple. Because it was “blood money,” the priests could not put it into the sacred treasury, so they officially used the funds to purchase the Potter’s Field to bury strangers in (Mt 27:6-7). On the other hand, Acts’ perspective is idiomatic and indirect. Luke writes that Judas “purchased a field with the reward of iniquity.” In ancient Jewish and Greco-Roman literature, a person was frequently said to have done something if they provided the money or cause for it to happen. Since the field was bought directly with Judas’ stolen silver, the land was legally and causally attributed to Judas.

Judas experienced overwhelming guilt (remorse), but he turned inward to suicide instead of turning outward to God in faith (repentance). Peter fell equally hard by denying Jesus three times, but Peter wept bitterly and sought the Lord, resulting in restoration and power at Pentecost. Sin promises satisfaction, but once committed, it leaves its victim empty, exposed, and hopeless. The silver Judas traded his soul for became the very money that bought his burial ground.

6.x: “And the chief priests took the silver pieces..”: The priests picked up the thirty shekels that Judas had thrown down onto the floor of the Sanctuary (naos). “...it is not lawful for to put them into the treasury…”: The “treasury” (Korbanas) housed the sacred gifts and tithes dedicated to God and the maintenance of the Temple. Under Mosaic protocol (derived from Deut 23:18), money gained through illicit, unholy, or tainted means could not be brought into the house of the Lord to fund holy things. “...because it is the price of blood”: The priests openly acknowledge that this silver was paid out to hire a betrayer and murder an innocent man.

7.x: “And they took counsel..”: The council held a legal consultation to decide how to handle the “blood money” without violating their ceremonial traditions. “..and bought with them the potter’s field..”: A “potter’s field” was a plot of land from which a potter had harvested all the useful clay. Once stripped of clay, the land was pocked with holes, strewn with broken shards of pottery, and rendered useless for agriculture (making it cheap enough to buy for thirty shekels). “..to bury strangers in”: “Strangers” (xenos) referred to Gentile travelers, foreign Jews, or destitute pilgrims who died while visiting Jerusalem for the feasts. Because they were unclean or uncircumcised, they could not be buried in sacred Jewish family tombs. The priests used the blood money to establish a public graveyard for the outcast, poor, unknown, or unclaimed by family.

8.x: “Wherefore that field was called, The field of blood…”: In Aramaic, the plot was called “Akeldama” (Acts 1:19 - Akel Dama, “Field of Blood”). It acquired this name for a dual reason: it was purchased with the “price of blood” paid to Judas, and it became the site where Judas’ own body burst open in his death (Acts 1:18). “...unto this day”: This historical footnote indicates that at the time Matthew composed his Gospel narrative, the plot of land still retained its ominous name in Jerusalem, standing as a visible monument to the betrayal of Christ.

9.x: “Then was fulfilled…”: Matthew highlights that the hypocritical decision of the chief priests was not an unplanned accident; it fulfilled the sovereign, prophetic script written centuries earlier (Zech 11:12). “And they took the thirty pieces of silver..”: The exact contract price paid for the Savior. “...the value of him that was valued, whom they of the children of Israel did value”: A biting, sarcastic expression highlighting the insulting, trivial assessment the leaders of Israel placed upon their own Messiah, rating the Son of God as worth no more than a common injured slave (Ex 21:32).

10.x: “And gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord appointed me”: Citing Zech 11:13 and “Lord” meaning YHWH. The money that was meant to be the reward for treason ultimately ended up purchasing a burial ground for unclean outcasts, exactly as God’s divine decree had ordained.

Why does Matthew attribute the prophecy of verses 9-10 to Jeremiah the prophet when the specific mention of thirty pieces of silver thrown to the potter appears in Zechariah 11:12-13 ("So they weighed for my price thirty pieces of silver. And the LORD said unto me, Cast it unto the potter: a goodly price that I was prized at of them. And I took the thirty pieces of silver, and cast them to the potter in the house of the LORD,” Zech 11:12-13 KJV)? Some ways to harmonize this are: (1) Composite/Blended Quotation: It was standard Jewish rabbinic practice to blend two related prophecies into a single citation. Matthew fuses Zechariah 11:12-13 (the 30 pieces of silver, the Temple, and the potter) with major themes from Jeremiah, like Jeremiah visiting the potter’s house to see the clay marred and refashioned (Jer 18:1-4) or Jeremiah buying a potter’s earthen flask, taking the elders and chiefs priests out to the Valley of Hinnom (where Akeldama is located), breaking the flask, and prophesying that the place will become a “valley of slaughter” and a burial place for the dead because they shed innocent blood (Jeremiah 19:1-11) or Jeremiah officially purchasing a field with silver pieces (Jer 32:6-9). When Jewish writers combined passages from a major prophet and a minor prophet, they customarily cited the naem of the greater/major prophet (Jeremiah) as the heading (Mark uses this exact method in Mk 1:2-3 combining Malachi 3:1 and Isaiah 40:3 under the name of “Isaiah”). (2) The Structure of the Hebrew Canon: In ancient Jewish manuscript scrolls, the division of the Prophets (Nevi’im) frequently placed Jeremiah first in the scroll order (before Ezekiel, Isaiah, or the Twelve Minor Prophets). The entire prophetic scroll was often cited by the name of its first book - the “Jeremiah Scroll.”

11.x: “And Jesus stood before the governor…”: The Creator of the universe stands bound as a prisoner before a cynical Roman official. Pilate sat on the “bema” (judgment seat), executing the authority of Caesar, yet it was the King of Kings who was truly presiding over history. “...and the governor asked him, saying, Art thou the King of the Jews?”: Before the Sanhedrin, the charge was religious (“blasphemy” for claiming to be the Son of God). But before Pilate, the Sanhedrin adapted the charge to a political one (sedition and treason against Rome; Lk 23:2). Pilate’s question emphasizes the political title: “Art thou the King of the Jews?” To Rome, anyone claiming to be an earthly king without Caesar’s sanction was guilty of treason (“crimen laesae maiestatis,” or “crime of injured majesty”). “...And Jesus said unto him, Thou sayest”: This is a direct translation of the Hebrew/Aramaic idiom (“Thous hast said it’), which means: “It is as you say; your words are correct.” In John’s expanded account (Jn 18:36-37), Jesus clarifies that while he is indeed a King, his “kingdom is not of this world.” He does not deny his royalty, but he strips it of political rebellion against Rome.

12.x: “And when he was accused of the chief priests and elders…”: Seeing that Jesus’ direct answer to Pilate did not immediately provoke Pilate to condemn him, the chief priests and elders unleashed a torrent of additional, frantic accusations (Lk 23:2,5). “...he answered nothing”: Faced with a barrage of false, malicious lies, Jesus maintained complete, dignified silence. He offered no self-defense, no angry rebuttals, and no plea for mercy.

13.x: “Then said Pilate unto him..”: Pilate was accustomed to criminal trials where accused men wept, pleaded, lied, bribed, or shouted back at their accusers to save their lives. “Hearest thou not how many things they witness against thee?”: Pilate was perplexed by Jesus’ absolute composure. He pressed Jesus to speak, giving him an opportunity to refute the charge made by the Sanhedrin.

14.x: “And he answered him to never a word…”: Jesus refused to break his silence to defend himself against their manufactured charges. “..insomuch that the governor marvelled greatly”: Pilate was a hardened Roman ruler accustomed to fear, manipulation, and power plays. Seeing a man, facing the most horrific execution known to the ancient world (crucifixion), display such calm, royal self-control astonished Pilate. Jesus’ silence was not the silence of guilt or weakness, but the majestic restraint of One who was voluntarily laying down his life for the world (Jn 10:18). Jesus’ refusal to offer a self-defense was a direct fulfillment of Isaiah’s messianic prophecy: “He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth” (Isa 53:7 KJV). Peter later reflected on this exact moment before Pilate, instructing believers how to face unjust persecution: "Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously" (1 Peter 2:23 KJV). Jesus did not speak in his own defense because he had not come to escape the cross; he had come to fulfill the Father’s redemptive plan. His silence before Pilate secured our voice before the judgement seat of God.

15.x: “Now at that feast the governor was wont to release…”: This refers to the Roman custom of amnesty (privilegium Paschale) practiced during the Passover in Jerusalem. To appease the tense Jewish population during a volatile national holiday, the Roman procurator would grant a pardon to one condemned prisoner chosen by the crowd.

16.x: The word “notorious” (episemos) means well-known, prominent, or infamous. Parallel accounts (Mk 15:7, Lk 23:19) reveal that Barabbas was an insurgent involved in a violent rebellion against Rome who had committed murder during the uprising. The name “Barabbas,” in Aramaic “Bar-Abba” literally translates to “Son of the Father” (Bar = son, Abba = father). This creates a striking theological parallel: the crowd is forced to choose between a violent man whose name literally means “son of the father,” and Jesus Christ, the true, eternal Son of the Father. To make things even stranger, the modern Bibles based on the CT, render this verse and verse 17 as “Jesus Barabbas” (which would mean “Jesus son of the Father”). Even though over 95% of Greek manuscripts only have “Barabbas” (this includes the oldest manuscripts available: Sinaiticus, Vaticanus, Alexandrinus, etc), modern Critical Text scholars decided to follow a 9th century manuscript (Codex Foridethi) and add “Jesus” to Barabbas’ name mainly because of patristic evidence. Origen, writing in the third century, discusses Mt 27:16-17 and says that in many copies Barabbas was also called “Jesus,” so they’d argue that “Jesus Barabbas” is the harder reading, therefore, it is more likely for it to have been omitted on purpose than added on purpose. IF “Jesus Barabbas” is the true reading, then Matthew would have created a deliberate theological irony: “Jesus, son of the father” being released while “Jesus, the true Son of the Father” is crucified. That connection is possible, but I tend to trust the Textus Receptus (TR) and Majority Text (MT) more than the modern Critical Text (CT), since the CT overcorrects and introduces errors into Scripture that break parallel passages like Matthew 19:17 (CT reads: “what are you asking me about WHAT is good?” even though all parallel passages and TR/MT read as “why do you call ME good?”) or John 1:18 (CT reads: “the only begotten GOD”, which creates a paradox (a self-contradicting statement) of a God being begotten, while the TR/MT read: “the only begotten SON,” which harmonizes perfectly with the rest of Scripture, as seen in Jn 3:16, 18; 1 Jn 5:20; Heb 1:3).

17.x: “Therefore when they were gathered together..”: The crowd gathered outside the Praetorium consisted of the general public, Jerusalem residents, and temple agitators mobilized by the chief priests. “...Whom will ye that I release unto you?”: Pilate hoped the public would choose Jesus. He framed the choice as a start, undeniable contrast: a violent criminal vs a popular teacher. “...Barabbas, or Jesus which is called Christ?”: Pilate uses the title “which is called Christ” (Messiah) to highlight who Jesus was. He assumed the masses who had welcomed Jesus into Jerusalem days earlier with “Hosanna” (Mt 21:9) would naturally prefer him over a notorious murderer.

18.x: “For he knew that for envy…”: Pilate was a cynical politician, but he was not stupid. He clearly recognized that Jesus was not a violent revolutionary threatening Rome; rather, the Sanhedrin was driven by envy (phthonos). Jesus’ popularity, authority, miracles, and exposure of religious corruption threatened the priests’ financial and political monopoly over the people.

19.x: “When he was set down on the judgement seat…”: The “bema” was the official judicial bench where a Roman magistrate delivered formal, binding legal verdicts. “..his wife sent unto him…”: Church tradition names Pilater’s wife “Claudia Procula.” It was highly unusual for a Roman wife to interrupt her husband during official judicial proceedings, emphasizing the divine urgency of her message. “...Have thou nothing to do with that just man”: God used a Gentile woman to deliver a prophetic warning to the governor. She explicitly testifies to the righteousness of Christ, calling him a “just man” (dikaios - righteous/innocent). “..for I have suffered many things this day in a dream because of him”: God supernaturally troubled her sleep with a disturbing dream regarding the consequences of condemning Jesus. Even in the court of Rome, divine testimony was given to Christ’s innocence.

20.x: “But the chief priests and elders persuaded the multitude..”: While Pilate hesitated on the judgement seat, the religious leaders worked the crowd, exploiting their nationalistic fervor. “..that they should ask Barabbas, and destroy Jesus”: They convinced the people that Barabbas (a violent zealot who actually fought against Roman rule) was a hero, whereas Jesus was a spiritual teacher who refused to lead a military rebellion against Caesar.

21.x: “Whether of the twain..”: (“Which of the two…”): Pilate puts the official question to the floor, expecting the crowd to demand Jesus’ freedom. “They said, Barabbas”: The tragic, decisive rejection. The crowd chose a murderer over the Giver of Life (Acts 3:14-15).

22.x: “What shall I do then with Jesus which is called Christ?”: This remains the pivotal question every human soul must answer. Pilate tried to pass the moral responsibility onto the crowd. “They all say unto him, Let him be crucified”: Crucifixion was a horrific Roman method of execution reserved for slaves, bandits, and traitors. It was designed to maximize pain and lingering public shame. The Jewish mob demanded the most brutal Gentile punishment available, fulfilling Jesus’ prophecy in Matthew 20:19: “And shall deliver him to the Gentiles to mock, and to scourge, and to crucify him: and the third day he shall rise again” (KJV).

23.x: “Why, what evil hath he done?”: For the third time, the Roman governor declares Jesus legally innocent (Lk 23:22). No charge could be proven against him. “But they cried out the more..”: Reason and justice were overwhelmed by mob rule and religious hysteria. Unable to name a crime, they simply shouted louder to drown out Pilate’s legal objections.

24.x: “When Pilate saw that he could prevail nothing..”: Pilate’s primary goal as governor was keeping order. A riot (tumult) during Passover could bring down the wrath of Emperor Tiberius upon his career. “..he took water, and washed his hands before the multitude…”: Washing hands was a symbolic Jewish ritual (Deut 21:6-7; Ps 26:6) used to claim innocence from a murder. Pilate adopted this local custom in a dramatic public gesture to disclaim moral guilt. “I am innocent of the blood of his just person: see ye to it”: Pilate tried to cleanse his hands, but he could not cleanse his heart. As the supreme judge in Judea, he possessed the sole legal authority to release Jesus. By caving to political pressure and handing an innocent man over to death, Pilate remained morally guilty.

Barabbas is a vivid, real-time illustration of substitutionary atonement. He was a condemned criminal waiting in a cell for his cross. Jesus took Barabbas’ cross, Barabbas was set free, and Christ died in the sinner’s place. Also, Pilate tried to remain neutral by washing his hands and letting the crowd decide, but refusing to defend Christ is deciding against him: “He that is not with me is against me; and he that gathereth not with me scattereth abroad” (Mt 27:25 KJV) & “Whosoever therefore shall confess me before men, him will I confess also before my Father which is in heaven. But whosoever shall deny me before men, him will I also deny before my Father which is in heaven” (Mt 10:32-33 KJV).

25.x: “Then answered all the people, and said, His blood be on us, and on our children”: The phrase “His blood be on us” means, in effect, “we accept responsibility for this man’s death.” This verse has been used throughout church history (most notoriously the Middle Ages and 20th century) to promote anti-Semitism and blame Jewish people collectively across generations for the death of Jesus. However, this verse SHOULD NOT be interpreted as a justification for blaming all Jews throughout history for Jesus’ death. Matthew’s own gospel makes the responsibility more complicated: the chief priests and elders deliberately sought Jesus’ death (Mt 26:3-4), Judas betrayed him (Mt 26:14-16), Pilate knowingly handed him over despite recognizing his innocence (Mt 27:24-26), the Roman soldiers actually carried out the crucifixion (Mt 27:26-31), and Scripture ultimately presents Jesus as voluntarily laying down his life (Jn 10:17-18). And Acts shows that Jesus’ death was according to God’s PREDETERMINED plan (Acts 2:23). So v.25 describes the crowd’s declaration of responsibility, but it shouldn’t be turned into an ethnic condemnation of every Jew. There is also a connection with Mt 23:35, where Jesus speaks of the blood of righteous people being upon that generation. Jesus specifically says: “all these things shall come upon THIS generation” (Mt 23:36 KJV). That makes the immediate judgement particularly relevant to the generation living in Jesus’ day, rather than an eternal curse upon every Jewish person.

26.x: “Then released he Barabbas unto them: and when he had scourged Jesus, he delivered him to be crucified”: This is the great substitution in the narrative. Barabbas is guilty and deserving punishment, while Jesus is innocent. This provides a powerful picture of the Gospel: the guilty person is released while the innocent one suffers in his place. The same principle appears explicitly in Isaiah: “he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities” (Isa 53:5 KJV) and “the LORD hath laid on him the iniquity of us all” (Isa 53:6 KJV).

27.x: “Then the soldiers of the governor took Jesus…”: Now the Roman soldiers take Jesus inside the governor’s headquarters. The “common hall” refers to the governor’s headquarters (praetorium). The soldiers are preparing to mock Jesus as a supposed king.

28.x: “..they stripped him, and put on him a scarlet robe”: The soldiers strip Jesus and dress him in royal-looking clothing. The scarlet robe is part of the mockery. They are pretending that Jesus is a king. They are mocking him for being King while he actually is a king. Jesus had already told Pilate: “My kingdom is not of this world” (Jn 18:36 KJV). The soldiers therefore create a parody of royalty: a robe, a crown, a scepter, and homage.

29.x: “..when they had platted a crown of thorns … a reed … and they bowed the knee before him … Hail, King of the Jews!”: Everything here is designed as mock royalty: Crown (but made of thorns); Scepter (a reed); Royal robe (the scarlet garment); Homage (bowing the knee); Royal proclamation (“Hail, King of the Jews!”). This has deeper symbolical meaning. After Adam sinned: “Thorns also and thistles shall it bring forth to thee” (Gen 3:18 KJV). Jesus, the sinless man, now wears the symbol of the curse. Paul later explains: “Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us” (Gal 3:13 KJV). Adam brought the curse, and Christ bears the curse. The crown represents mockery and suffering becomes a picture of Christ bearing the consequences of sin.

30.x: “..they spit upon him, and took the reed, and smote him..”: The humiliation becomes physical abuse. Jesus had actually predicted this treatment: “And they shall mock him, and shall scourge him, and shall spit upon him, and shall kill him” (Mk 10:34 KJV). And Isaiah had prophesied: “I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting” (Isa 50:6 KJV). Jesus therefore isn’t merely unexpectedly experiencing humiliation. The Gospel writers present his suffering as the fulfillment of the prophetic picture of the suffering servant.

31.x: “..after they had mocked him, they took the robe off..and led him away to crucify him”: The mock coronation ends. They remove the scarlet robe and put his own clothes back on him. Then “led him away to crucify him.” Now the humiliation moves from the governor’s headquarters to Golgotha.

32.x: “And as they came out…” Execution of condemned criminals was forbidden inside the city walls under both Jewish ceremonial law (Lev 24:14; Heb 13:12) and Roman custom. They marched Jesus outside the gates of Jerusalem. “..they found a man of Cyrene, Simon by name..”: Cyrene was a Greek city in North Africa (modern-day Libya) with a large Jewish population. Simon had likely traveled over 800 miles to Jerusalem as a pilgrim to celebrate the Passover feast. “..him they compelled to bear his cross”: A condemned prisoner was required by Roman law to carry the heavy crossbar (patibulum) across his own neck to the site of execution. Having lost substantial blood and stamina under the brutal Roman scourging (flagellum), Jesus’ human frame collapsed under the weight. The Roman soldiers exercised their legal right of “impressment” (angareuo - the authority to commandeer a civilian or subject for forced labor) to force Simon to pick up the wood and carry it behind Jesus. Mark 15:21 notes that Simon was the father of Alexander and Rufus, suggesting his family later became prominent members of the early Christian Church (Rom 16:13).

33.x: “And when they were come unto a place called Golgotha..”: Golgotha is the Aramaic word for “skull” (transliterated into Latin as “Calvaria,” from which we get the English word “Calvary”). “...that is to say, a place of a skull”: The location was named this either because the rocky hillside naturally resembled the shape of a human skull (a feature visible at the traditional Gordon’s Calvary outside the Northern wall); or perhaps it was a well-known public place of execution littered with unburied remains or history of condemned men.

34.x: “They gave him vinegar to drink mingled with gall…”: This mixture was sour wine or wine-vinegar (posca) blended with a bitter narcotic herb (gall or myrrh, Mk 15:23). According to Jewish tradition recorded in the Talmud (Sanhedrin 43a), wealthy women of Jerusalem provided a stupifying, narcotic drink to condemned prisoners before crucifixion to numb their senses and deaden the agonizing pain. “..and when he had tasted thereof, he would not drink”: Jesus tasted it to acknowledge the human gesture, but he refused to drink it. He chose to face the agony on the cross with a clear, conscious mind, fully experiencing the penalty for human sin without any narcotic escape or self-anesthetization. This act directly fulfilled Psalm 69:21: “They gave me also gall for my meat; and in my thirst they gave me vinegar to drink” (KJV).

35.x: “And they crucified him..”: Crucifixion was considered the most painful, humiliating form of execution in the ancient world, reserved for foreign rebels, slaves, and low-class criminals. The prisoner was stretched across the wooden frame, heavy iron spikes were driven through the wrists and feet, and the cross was lifted and dropped into a socket in the ground, causing severe joint dislocation, shock, and gradual asphyxiation. “..and parted his garments, casting lots..”: It was standard Roman legal practice for the execution squad (a quaternion of four soldiers; Jn 19:23) to divide the personal property of the condemned prisoner among themselves as spoils (spolia). They gambled (cast lots, likely using dice or marked stones) for his seamless tunic. “...that it might be fulfilled which was spoken by the prophet..”: Matthew identifies this scene as the literal, precise fulfillment of Psalm 22:18, written by King David roughly a thousand years earlier: “They part my garments among them, and cast lots upon my vesture” (Ps 22:18 KJV).

Simon of Cyrene physically fulfilled what Jesus commanded his followers to do spiritually in Mt 16:24: “If any man will come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (KJV).

Jesus was stripped naked of his earthly garments so that through his death and resurrection, believers could be clothed in the garments of salvation and the righteousness of God: “I will greatly rejoice in the LORD(YHWH), my soul shall be joyful in my God; for he hath CLOTHED ME with the garments of salvation, he hath covered me with the robe of righteousness, as a bridegroom decketh himself with ornaments, and as a bride adorneth herself with her jewels” (Isa 61:10 KJV); and we accept his garments by becoming his disciple through repentance and baptism: “For ye are all the children of God by faith in Christ Jesus. For as many of you AS HAVE BEEN BAPTIZED INTO CHRIST HAVE PUT ON CHRIST (as garments of righteousness). There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither bond nor free, there is neither male nor female: for ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Gal 3:26-28 KJV).

36.x: “And sitting down..”: The four Roman soldiers assigned to the execution squad (quaternion) sat at the base of the cross. Having divided his clothing and cast lots for his tunic (v.35), their physical work was largely complete. “...they watched him there”: They kept guard over the site to ensure no sympathetic followers or onlookers attempted to rescue him or take him down before death occurred.

37.x: “And set up over his head…”: It was standard Roman legal procedure to display the official charge against a condemned person. The placard (titulus) was carried in front of the prisoner on the way to execution or hung around his neck, and then affixed to the top of the cross above his head. “..his accusation written…”: Under Roman law, a person could only be executed for a specific crime. Because Pilate found no moral fault or civil crime in Jesus, the only “accusation” the religious leaders could produce was his claim to be the Messianic King. “...THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS”: Pilate intended this inscription as a sharp sarcastic insult aimed directly at the chief priests who had blackmailed him into ordering the execution. To Pilate, it mocked their national hopes: “Here is your king, bloody and dying on a Roman cross.” Unknowingly, Pilate posted a true, divine declaration: Jesus was indeed the long-awaited King of Israel and sovereign Lord of all.

Another frequent attack on Scripture is the variation in the text of the sign across the four Gospel accounts. However, when examined historically and textually, these four accounts fit together seamlessly. For four Gospel accounts: (1) Matthew 27:37: “THIS IS JESUS THE KING OF THE JEWS;” (2) Mark 15:26: “THE KING OF THE JEWS;” (3) Luke 23:38: “THIS IS THE KING OF THE JEWS;” (3) John 19:19: “JESUS OF NAZARETH THE KING OF THE JEWS.” An easy way to harmonize these discrepancies is that the sign was written in three languages. John 19:20 provides the critical historical key: “and it was written in Hebrew, and Greek, and Latin.” Because a single statement translated across three distinct ancient languages naturally carries slight stylistic variations, the Gospel writers were translating or citing different language panels from the same tri-lingual board. Hence, every single Gospel includes the core, indispensable charge: “THE KING OF THE JEWS.” None of the Gospel writers contradict one another; rather, each provides a precise excerpt or summary of the full title. When all four accounts are combined, the complete text on the board read: “THIS IS JESUS OF NAZARETH, THE KING OF THE JEWS.” In John 19:21-22, the chief priests were furious that Pilate wrote “The King of the Jews” as a statement of fact, asking him to change it to “He said, I am King of the Jews.” Pilate famously replied: “What I have written I have written,” preserving the royal witness over the cross for all humanity (Greek, Latin, Hebrew) to read. By posting the charge in Hebrew, Latin, and Greek, God ensured that religion (Hebrew), civil law/government (Latin), and human philosophy/culture (Greek) were all confronted with the kingship of Jesus Christ. His cross speaks to every culture, tribe, and tongue.

Jesus is the first person in human history to pass through death into an eternal, glorified resurrection body. “..and went into the holy city..”: This is the standard biblical title for Jerusalem (Mt 4:5; Isa 48:2). “...and appeared unto many..”: This was not a secret or hallucinated phenomenon; these resurrected individuals openly entered Jerusalem and walked among its inhabitants as eye-witness testimonies. Nothing more is said about these people, suggesting that they did not remain on earth for long. Evidently, these people were given glorified bodies; they appeared “to many”, enough to establish the reality of the miracle; and then they ascended to glory, a kind of foretaste of 1 Thess 4:16: “For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first” (KJV).

54.x: “Now when the centurion, and they that were with him, watching Jesus…”: A Roman centurion was an officer in command of approximately 100 soldiers. He and his execution squad were stationed at the cross to carry out the death sentence and ensure no rescue attempts occurred. “..saw the earthquake, and those things that were done, they feared greatly..”: These hardened, pagan Roman soldiers were accustomed to violent deaths, but the unique cosmic disruptions (three hours of supernatural darkness, the earthquake, and the victorious manner in which Jesus died) struck profound terror into their hearts. “..saying, Truly this was the Son of God”: This stands as a dramatic climax in Matthew’s Gospel. While Israel’s religious leaders mocked Jesus as a pretender (v.43), a pagan Roman military commander became the first person at the foot of the cross to confess Jesus as the Son of God.

55.x: “And many women were there beholding afar off…”: While most of the male disciples had fled in fear (Mt 26:56), a group of devoted women remained present near Golgotha. They stood at a distance, likely due to Roman guard perimeters and safety concerns. “...which followed Jesus from Galilee, ministering unto him”: These women were not casual onlookers; they were long-term disciples who had traveled with him from northern Galilee, providing financial support, food, and care for Jesus and his apostles throughout his ministry (Lk 8:1-3).

56.x: “Among which was Mary Magdalene..”: Mary from the town of Magdala. She is consistently named first in the Gospel lists of women, signifying her leadership and prominent role as a witness. Jesus had cast seven demons out of her (Lk 8:2), and her deep devotion kept her at the cross and brought her first to the empty tomb on East morning. “...and Mary the mother of James and Joses..”: A key female disciple identified by her sons to distinguish her from Mary the mother of Jesus, and Mary Magdalene. As demonstrated across the parallel accounts, this is Mary of Clopas (early church tradition, Hegesippus, says she is the sister-in-law of Joseph and aunt of Jesus), and her son is James the Less (Mk 15:40), one of the Twelve Apostles. “..and the mother of Zebedee’s children”: The mother of the apostles James (the Greater who was the first to be martyred) and John, the beloved disciple (Mt 10:2). In Mt 20:20-23, she approached Jesus asking for her two sons to sit at his right and left hands in his kingdom. Cross-referencing Mk 15:40 reveals her proper name: Salome. John’s parallel account shows: (1) Jesus’ “mother, and (2) his mother’s sister, (3) Mary the wife of Cleophas, and (4) Mary Magdalene” (Jn 19:25 KJV). Since we know for sure who Jesus’ mother & Mary Magdalene are, the most probable harmonization of the gospels is that (3) “Mary the wife of Cleophas” is the mother of James and Joses(v.56), and “Salome” is (2) the sister of Mary the mother of Jesus. This means that James the Greater and John (the beloved disciple) are Jesus’ first cousins.

The women described at the cross by the different Gospel authors: (1) Matthew 27:55-56: (a) Mary Magdalene; (b) Mary the mother of James and Joses; (c) The mother of Zebedee’s children. (2) Mark 15:40-41: (a) Mary Magdalene; (b) Mary the mother of James the less and Joses; (c) Salome. (3) Luke 23:49, 24:10: (a) Mary Magdalene; (b) Mary the mother of James; (c) Joanna; (d) “Other women that were with them” / “Women that followed him from Galilee” (4) John 19:25: (a) His mother [Mary, mother of Jesus]; (b) His mother’s sister; (c) Mary the wife of Clopas (Cleophas); (d) Mary Magdalene.

57.x: “When the even was come…”: Jewish law mandated that executed criminals could not remain hanging on a tree overnight (Deut 21:22-23). Furthermore, because the Sabbath began at sunset (around 6:00 PM), the burial had to occur swiftly before the holy day commenced. “..there came a rich man of Arimathea, named Joseph…”: Arimathea was a Jewish town (likely the OT Ramathaim-zophim, birthplace of Samuel). Mark 15:43 adds that Joseph was an honorable member of the Sanhedrin, though Luke 23:51 clarifies he had not consented to their vote against Jesus. “..who also himself was Jesus’ disciple”: John 19:38 notes he was a disciple “secretly for fear of the Jews.” Jesus’ death acted as the catalyst that forced Joseph out of hiding to take a public stand for his Master.

58.x: “He went to Pilate, and begged the body of Jesus”: Standard Roman practice for executed rebels (perduellio) was to leave their bodies on the cross to rot or throw them into a common grave for criminals. It took immense courage for Joseph to approach the Roman Governor Pontius Pilate. Requesting the body aligned Joseph directly with a man condemned for treason against Rome, threatening his wealth, status, and seat on the Sanhedrin. “Then Pilate commanded the body to be delivered”: Mark 15:44-45 records that Pilate was surprised Jesus was already dead and confirmed it with the centurion before releasing the body to Joseph.

59.x: “And when Joseph had taken the body..”: Cross-referencing John 19:39, Joseph was joined by Nicodemus (another secret disciple on the Sanhedrin), who brought roughly 100 pounds of myrrh and aloes to prepare the body. “...he wrapped it in a clean linen cloth”: “Linen cloth” (sindōn) was fine, expensive linen sheet. Wrapping the body with burial spices was the customary Jewish preparation for honorable burial, ensuring the body was handled with reverence rather than cast into a mass grave.

60.x: “And laid it in his own new tomb, which he had hewn out in the rock..”: John 19:41 specifies that no one had ever been laid in this “new tomb” before. This detail rules out any claims that Jesus’ eventual resurrection was confused with another corpse in the tomb. This fulfills Isaiah 53:9 written over 700 years earlier: “And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death.” Jesus died among criminals, but was buried in a wealthy ruler’s tomb. “...and he rolled a great stone to the door of the sepulchre, and departed”: Rock-hewn tombs were secured by a large, heavy stone(golel) rolled along a slanted groove to block the entrance from tomb robbers and animals. Joseph’s tomb provided an exact, known location for both the Roman guards (vv 62-66) and the Galilean women to monitor, ensuring there was no confusion about which tomb was found empty on Easter morning. Jesus literally died. He did not merely faint or swoon on the cross; he died and was formally prepared for burial by two high-ranking Jewish leaders.

61.x: “And there was Mary Magdalene, and the other Mary…”: As established earlier (Mt 27:56, Jn 19:25), the “other Mary” was Mary of Clopas, mother of James the Less and Joses. “...sitting over against the sepulchre”: While Joseph of Arimathea and Nicodemus prepared and sealed the tomb, these women sat directly opposite the entrance. They took careful mental note of the precise physical location where Jesus was placed (Mk 15:47) so they could return after the Sabbath with additional spices (Lk 23:56).

62.x: “Now the next day, that followed the day of the preparation..”: The “day of preparation” was Friday (the day before the Sabbath, when Passover preparations took place). “The next day” means Saturday, the Jewish Sabbath. “..the chief priests and Pharisees came together unto Pilate”: the religious leaders were so consumed by fear that they broke their own strict Sabbath regulations to conduct business with a pagan ROman governor, securing a legal order on a holy day.

63.x: “Saying, Sir, we remember that that deceiver said..”: They contemptuously label Jesus a “deceiver” (planot- a fraud or imposter). “...while he was yet alive, After three days I will rise again”: ironically, Christ’s enemies understood his predictions of resurrection (Mt 12:40; 16:21; 20:19) far more clearly at this moment than his own scattered disciples did. They took his words seriously enough to guard against any potential fulfillment.

64.x: “Command therefore that the sepulchre be made sure until the third day…”: they demand Roman authorization to secure the tomb through the three-day window to prevent any fraudulent claims. “...lest his disciples come by night, and steal him away…”: they anticipated a staged resurrection, worrying the disciples would spirit the body away and proclaim him risen. “...so the last error shall be worse than the first”: the “first error” was people believing Jesus was the promised Messiah during his living ministry. The “last error” is people believing he rose from the dead. They recognized that a risen Messiah would ignite an unstoppable movement far greater than his earthly ministry.

65.x: “Pilate said unto them, Ye have a watch…”: the phrase (echete koustōdian) can mean either “Take a Roman guard” or “Use your existing Temple guard.” The BSB translates it as: “You have a guard… Go, make the tomb as secure as you know how.” Most scholars agree Pilate assigned a Roman guard unit (koustōdia), consisting of 4 to 16 heavily armed Roman soldiers. “..go your way, make it as sure as ye can’: Pilate gives them full authority to use whatever security measures they deem necessary to make the tomb completely unbreachable.

66.x: “So they went, and made the sepulchre sure…”: the Jewish leaders took full advantage of Pilate’s decree to secure the tomb via two distinct Roman mechanisms: (1) “sealing the stone” (sphragisantes): a string or cord was stretched across the large rolling stone and anchored on both sides of the rock face with soft clay or wax, stamped with the official imperial seal of Rome. Breaking this seal carried the immediate death penalty under Roman law. (2) “setting a watch”: stationing the Roman guard around the tomb to keep vigil day and night. By placing hostile Roman guards at the tomb, the Sanhedrin inadvertently provided unbiased, non-Christian witnesses who would later report the supernatural earthquake and the angel on Sunday morning (Mt 28:11-15). The combination of a massive stone, an unbroken Roman seal, and a detachment of Roman soldiers completely destroyed any argument that the disciples could have slipped past, broken in, and stolen the corpse.
